title: LIKE Operator
description: Learn how to use the LIKE operator to check if a character string matches a specified pattern using wildcard characters.

data.text: The SQL Server LIKE operator is a logical operator that checks if a character string matches a specified pattern.
A pattern may include regular characters and wildcard characters. The LIKE operator is used in the WHERE clause of the SELECT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements to filter rows based on pattern matching.

data.title: LIKE Syntax
data.content: Match a column or expression against a pattern.

data.text: A pattern can include the following valid wildcard characters:

items: % (percent): matches any string of zero or more characters.
[list of characters]: matches any single character within the specified set.
[character-character]: matches any single character within the specified range.
[^]: matches any character that is not within a list or a range.

data.text: The wildcard characters make the LIKE operator more flexible than the equal (=) and not equal (!=) string comparison operators.
The escape character instructs the LIKE operator to treat wildcard characters as regular characters. The escape character has no default value and must evaluate to exactly one character.
To negate the LIKE operator, use the NOT operator:

data.title: NOT LIKE Syntax
data.content: NOT LIKE returns rows that do not match the pattern.
data.code: column | expression NOT LIKE pattern [ESCAPE escape_character]

data.title: Last Name Starting with 'z'
data.content: Find customers whose last name starts with the letter z.
data.code:
SELECT
    customer_id,
    first_name,
    last_name
FROM
    sales.customers
WHERE
    last_name LIKE 'z%'
ORDER BY
    first_name;

data.title: Last Name Ending with 'er'
data.content: Find customers whose last name ends with 'er'.
data.code:
SELECT
    customer_id,
    first_name,
    last_name
FROM
    sales.customers
WHERE
    last_name LIKE '%er'
ORDER BY
    first_name;

data.title: Last Name Starting with 't' and Ending with 's'
data.content: Use % as a wildcard in the middle of the pattern.
data.code:
SELECT
    customer_id,
    first_name,
    last_name
FROM
    sales.customers
WHERE
    last_name LIKE 't%s'
ORDER BY
    first_name;

data.title: _u% Pattern
data.content: The first underscore matches any single character, 'u' matches the letter u, and % matches any sequence.
data.code:
SELECT
    customer_id,
    first_name,
    last_name
FROM
    sales.customers
WHERE
    last_name LIKE '_u%'
ORDER BY
    first_name;

data.title: [YZ] Pattern
data.content: Match last names starting with Y or Z.
data.code:
SELECT
    customer_id,
    first_name,
    last_name
FROM
    sales.customers
WHERE
    last_name LIKE '[YZ]%'
ORDER BY
    last_name;

data.title: [A-C] Pattern
data.content: Match last names starting with a letter in the range A through C.
data.code:
SELECT
    customer_id,
    first_name,
    last_name
FROM
    sales.customers
WHERE
    last_name LIKE '[A-C]%'
ORDER BY
    first_name;

data.title: [^A-X] Pattern
data.content: Match last names starting with a letter NOT in the range A through X.
data.code:
SELECT
    customer_id,
    first_name,
    last_name
FROM
    sales.customers
WHERE
    last_name LIKE '[^A-X]%'
ORDER BY
    last_name;

data.title: NOT LIKE - Names Not Starting with 'A'
data.content: Find customers whose first name does not start with the letter A.
data.code:
SELECT
    customer_id,
    first_name,
    last_name
FROM
    sales.customers
WHERE
    first_name NOT LIKE 'A%'
ORDER BY
    first_name;

data.text: The ESCAPE clause is useful when you need to search for wildcard characters themselves in the data. For example, to search for the literal string '30%' in a comment:

data.title: Searching for Literal Percent Sign
data.content: Use ESCAPE to treat % as a literal character instead of a wildcard.
data.code:
SELECT
    feedback_id,
    comment
FROM
    sales.feedbacks
WHERE
    comment LIKE '%30!%%' ESCAPE '!';

data.title: ESCAPE Clause
data.text: In this query, the ESCAPE clause specifies that the character '!' is the escape character. It instructs the LIKE operator to treat the % character as a literal string instead of a wildcard.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: The LIKE operator checks if a character string matches a specified pattern.
Use wildcard characters: % for any sequence, _ for a single character, [] for character sets and ranges.
Use NOT LIKE to find strings that do not match the pattern.
Use the ESCAPE clause to search for literal wildcard characters in data.
LIKE is more flexible than equal/not equal comparisons for string matching.
